Lakhan Lal
 Versus
 The State Of Madhya Pradesh And Others
 Appearance:

 Shri Harjeet Singh - Advocate for respondent No.2.
 Order

The present petition is filed by the petitioner under Section 528 of the Bhartiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, invoking the inherent powers of this Court, seeking quashing of FIR dated 20.02.2025 registered at Police Station Ranjhi, District Jabalpur (M.P.), bearing Crime No.128/2025 for the offences punishable under Sections 376 and 376(2)(n) of the IPC and all other consequential proceedings.

2. As per the prosecution case, the complainant/victim lodged a report on 20.02.2025 at Police Station Ranjhi, District Jabalpur, stating that the complainant and the petitioner were classmates at Government ITI in the year 2014.

They developed a love relationship, and on 19.09.2015, for the first time, the applicant established physical relations with the complainant on the false pretext of marriage at the house of his relative.
Thereafter, NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-JBP:2832 2 MCRC-13732-2025 physical relations were established on several occasions.
It is further alleged that in June 2024, the petitioner took the complainant to Narmada Hotel, Gwarighat Road, and again established physical relations with her.
On that basis police registered FIR against the petitioner.
3. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the petitioner is a Central Government employee working in the Railways as a Factory Assistant.
The petitioner never gave any allurement to the complainant to marry her.
The complaint lodged by the complainant is false and fabricated.

Moreover, there is an almost 10-year delay in lodging the FIR, and no plausible explanation has been given for such delay.
4.
It is further submitted that the petitioner and the complainant were friends.

The petitioner never Lakhan Lal vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 6 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/173409107/
1 gave assurance of marriage to the complainant.

sentences.text: However, when the petitioner joined the central government service, then the complainant made pressure to perform marriage with her otherwise, she will implicate the petitioner in false and frivolous cases.
5. Furthermore, it is submitted that, as per the FIR, the first alleged incident occurred on 19.09.2015, while the last alleged incident is stated to have taken place in June 2024.

The FIR,
however, was lodged only in February 2025, after a delay of approximately eight months from the last incident.
No plausible or satisfactory explanation has been given for this delay in lodging the FIR.
It is also submitted that, on a plain reading of the FIR, no offence is made out.
The allegations pertain entirely to matters of consent and, therefore, the FIR is liable to be quashed.

6 . Per contra, learned counsel for the State has opposed the prayer and NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2026:MPHC-JBP:2832 3 MCRC-13732-2025 submitted that there are direct allegations against the petitioner, therefore, the FIR and pending proceedings may not be quashed.
7. Counsel for the respondent No.2. submits that the petitioner committed the aforementioned offences on the basis of false promise of marriage.
If a woman engaged herself in sexual relation on false promise, her consent would be treated to be a consent given under misconception of fact and such a consent would amount to rape.
Therefore, present petition deserves to be dismissed as there are directed allegations against the petitioner.

8. Heard rival submissions and perused the record.
9.
The FIR registered against the present petitioner reveals that at the time of the first alleged incident, both the parties were friends and had subsequently fallen in love.
It is submitted that on 19.09.2015, the petitioner took the complainant to his relative's vacant house at Ranjhi, where he disclosed to her that he loved her and intended to marry her.
Thereafter, it is alleged that physical relations took place between the petitioner and the complainant.
It is further submitted that subsequently, the petitioner allegedly took the complainant to various hotels, where physical relations occurred.
However, when the complainant asked the petitioner to marry her, he allegedly made excuses and did not solemnize the marriage.

It is also mentioned in the FIR that in June 2024,
the petitioner took the complainant to Hotel Narmada at Gwarighat Road and made physical relations.
This was the last time when they met before lodging of FIR.
The FIR was lodged in February, 2025 i.e. 8 months after the last incident.

10. The foremost question for adjudication is that whether the petitioner NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2026:MPHC-JBP:2832 4 MCRC-13732-2025 was engaged in physical relation with the complainant on false pretext of marriage and thereafter her consent being obtained on misconception of facts and false promise of marriage.

11. It is well settled principle that consent of woman with respect to Section 375 of IPC must involve an active and reasoned deliberations towards the proposed acts to establish whether the consent was Lakhan Lal vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 6 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/173409107/
2

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: vitiated by misconception of fact arising out of promise to marry, two prepositions must be established.
The promise of marriage must have been a false promise, given in bad faith and with no intention to being adhered to at the time it was given.
The false promise itself must be of immediate relevance, or bear a direct nexus to the woman's decision to engage in the sexual act.
It is also established that a breach of a promise cannot be said to be a false promise.

12. In this regard reference can be had of a decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Maheshwar Tigga v. State of Jharkhand reported in (2020) 10 SCC 108 wherein it is held - "13- The question for our consideration is whether the prosecutrix consented to the physical relationship under any misconception of fact with regard to the promise of marriage by the appellant or was her consent based on a fraudulent misrepresentation of marriage which the appellant never intended to keep since the very inception of the relationship.

entities.text: Maheshwar Tigga v. State of Jharkhand reported in (2020) 10 SCC 108
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: If we reach the conclusion that he intentionally made a fraudulent misrepresentation from the very inception and the prosecutrix gave her consent on a misconception of fact, the offence of rape under Section 375 IPC is clearly made out.
It is not possible to hold in the nature of evidence on record that the appellant obtained her consent at the inception by putting her under any fear.
Under Section 90 IPC a consent given under fear of injury is not a consent in the eyes of law.

In the facts of the present case we are not persuaded to accept the solitary statement of the prosecutrix that at the time of the first alleged offence her consent was obtained under fear of injury."
13.
As per record and contents of FIR there is no evidence of coercion or threat or injury to the complainant.

It is also cannot be ignored that from the NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2026:MPHC-JBP:2832 5 MCRC-13732-2025 year 2014 to 2020 the complainant visited various hotels with the petitioner and made physical relation without any threat or coercion.

NEUTRAL CITATION NO.

sentences.text: Even if the allegation in the FIR are taken as true and correct, it does not appear from the record that the consent of the complainant was obtained against her will merely on assurance of marriage.

The petitioner and the complainant were acquainted since 2014 and the complainant has admitted that they interacted frequently and fell in love and made physical relation at various hotels of Jabalpur.

The allegation of the complainant that the petitioner made physical relation without her consent is also not found true because she not only sustained her relationship for over 10 years but continued to visit in various hotels on several occasions.
The narration of the complainant in the FIR does not corroborate with her conduct.
14. Therefore, the consent of complainant as defined under Section 90 of IPC also cannot be said to have been under the misconception of fact.
There is no material to substantiate inducement or misrepresentation on the part of the petitioner to secure consent of physical relation without having any intention of fulfilling said promise.

15. In Maheshwar Tigga (supra) it is held- Lakhan Lal vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 6 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/173409107/
3 "

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 1 4 - Under Section 90 IPC, a consent given under a misconception of fact is no consent in the eyes of law.
But the misconception of fact has to be in proximity of time to the occurrence and cannot be spread over a period of four years.

It hardly needs any elaboration that the consent by the appellant was a conscious and informed choice made by her after due deliberation, it being spread over a long period of time coupled with a conscious positive action not to protest.

The prosecutrix in her letters to the appellant also mentions that there would often be NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-JBP:2832 6 MCRC-13732-2025 quarrels at her home with her family members with regard to the relationship, and beatings given to her."
15. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Amol Bhagwan v. State of Maharashtra : AIR 2025 SC 2629 has held- "9-

entities.text: Amol Bhagwan v. State of Maharashtra : AIR 2025 SC 2629
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In our considered view, this is also not a case where there was a false promise to marry to begin with.
A consensual relationship turning sour or partners becoming distant cannot be a ground for invoking criminal machinery of the State.
Such conduct not only burdens the Courts, but blots the identity of an individual accused of such a heinous offence.

This Court has time and again warned against the misuse of the provisions, and has termed it a folly to treat each breach of promise to marry as a false promise and prosecute a person for an offence under section 376 IPC."

16. Taking into consideration all the facts and circumstances of the case, it is clearly reflected that neither in the FIR nor in the statement of the complainant, anywhere it is mentioned that when complainant refused to make physical relation then the petitioner obtained her consent on the false pretext of marriage.

Apart from that, as per the FIR the last incident occurred in June 2024,
however, the FIR was lodged in February 2025 i.e. almost eight months later.
There is no reason afforded for the delay.
17. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of State of Haryana and others v. Bhajanlal and others [(1992) Supp 1 SCC 335 ]. has held as under - "102.

entities.text: State of Haryana and others v. Bhajanlal and others [(1992) Supp 1 SCC 335 ]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In the backdrop of the interpretation of the various relevant provisions of the Code under Chapter XIV and of the principles of law enunciated by this Court in a series of decisions relating to the exercise of the extraordinary power under Article 226 or the inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code which we have extracted and reproduced above, we give the following categories of cases by way of illustration wherein such power could be exercised either to prevent abuse of the process of any court or NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-JBP:2832 7 MCRC-13732-2025 otherwise to secure the ends of justice, though it may not be possible to lay down any precise, clearly defined and sufficiently channelised and inflexible guidelines or rigid formulae and to give an exhaustive list of myriad kinds of cases wherein such power should be exercised.

Lakhan Lal vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 6 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/173409107/
4 (1) Where the allegations made in the first information report or the complaint, even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety do not prima facie constitute any offence or make out a case against the accused.
(2) Where the allegations in the first information report and other materials, if any,
accompanying the FIR do not disclose a cognizable offence, justifying an investigation by police officers under Section 156(1) of the Code except under an order of a Magistrate within the purview of Section 155(2) of the Code.

entities.text: Lakhan Lal vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: ( 3 ) Where the uncontroverted allegations made in the FIR or complaint and the evidence collected in support of the same do not disclose the commission of any offence and make out a case against the accused.

(4) Where, the allegations in the FIR do not constitute a cognizable offence but constitute only a non-cognizable offence, no investigation is permitted by a police officer without an order of a Magistrate as contemplated under Section 155(2) of the Code.

(5) Where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint are so absurd and inherently improbable on the basis of which no prudent person can ever reach a just conclusion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused.

18. When the above mentioned facts as mentioned in the FIR and the record are taken into consideration, this Court is of the considered opinion that the present case is squarely covered by the judgement of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Bhajalal (supra).
Moreover, this petition is filed seeking exorcise of extraordinary jurisdiction for quashment of the FIR and NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-JBP:2832 8 MCRC-13732-2025 consequential proceedings.

Therefore,
considering the facts in its entirety, this Court has no hesitation to hold that the FIR amounts to abuse of the process of law, therefore, the FIR dated 20.02.2025 registered at Police Station Ranjhi,
District Jabalpur (M.P.), bearing Crime No.128/2025 for the offences punishable under Sections 376 and 376(2)(n) of the IPC and all other consequential proceedings, stands quashed.
18. The present petitioner is discharged of the charges framed against him.
Bail bond if executed by the petitioner also stand discharged.
19. Accordingly, the petition stands allowed.
